items.title: I got my start writing for a PlayStation 2 magazine: These are my 12 PS2-pilled recommendations from the Steam Autumn Sale
items.author: Samuel Roberts

items.text:
What's great about the PS2 back catalogue is that it's too vast to have an encyclopedic knowledge of everything in there. The defining 20 or so games on the platform—God of War, Gran Turismo 3, Final Fantasy 10 and so forth—are very well known, and maybe Millennial players can recall a weirdo game or two like Mr Mosquito or Global Defence Force. One look at the games in the Japan-only Simple 2000 series, however, shows you just how deep the library goes. When's Demolition Girl getting a HD remaster, eh?

Still, we're in an era where it's not hard to rediscover the key games of that generation, partly because many platform highlights have found their way to Steam in various forms. Intriguingly, we've also reached a point where developers who grew up with this generation are designing great new games inspired by the classics.

Below you'll find six modern games that are inspired by what's known as the 'sixth generation' of consoles, plus six ports of Dreamcast/PS2/GameCube/Xbox-era favourites. I've kept the latter to games that didn't get a PC release at the time (so GTA: San Andreas would be ineligible, for example). All of the games in both lists are discounted in the Steam Autumn Sale.

PS2-inspired

Promise Mascot Agency

(Image credit: Kaizen Game Works)Promise Mascot Agency (40% off at $15/£13) is an open world game built around a novel management simulation layer. You send Japanese mascots off to various events while exploring an island that may or may not be cursed. It's actually one of the better open world games of recent years because every sidequest offers something meaningful, like additional mascots to manage or upgrades for your truck (culminating in flight capabilities, as pictured). It's also deeply PS2-pilled in its overall presentation, with its creators citing everything from Disaster Report to Persona 4 as its influences. "6 and 7 out of 10 PS2 games are what I live for," director Oli Clarke Smith told RPG Site. It shows in the marvellously unique finished product.

Hi-Fi Rush

(Image credit: Tango Gameworks)Hi-Fi Rush (55% off at £12.14/$13.49) is at the intersection of several great PS2-era phenomena: innovative rhythm action games, cel-shaded visuals and Devil May Cry-style 3D hack-and-slash combat. Tango Gameworks weaves in many other influences besides, including the way director Edgar Wright matches music to visuals in films like Shaun of the Dead and Baby Driver. It's not exactly at DMC or Bayonetta's level when it comes to hardcore combat credentials, but it's presented in an appealing and often breathtaking anime wrapping, and playing to the beat sets it apart. It captures the flavour of the PS2 era without being exactly like any single game.

Denshattack!

(Image credit: Undercoders)A leading candidate for my top 10 games of 2026, Denshattack! (25% off at $15/£12) draws inspiration from Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, but perhaps more crucially, blue skies Dreamcast classics like Crazy Taxi and Jet Set Radio. It's a speedrunning game of stunt jumping, grinding and rapidly boosting your train through regions of a corporate-owned version of Japan. Except the vision of it just keeps expanding, until you're eventually using said train to battle enormous robots and smash massive baseballs at bosses. Again, it's not exactly like any one of its inspirations—this is a special game because the developers draw something original from those sources.

Sifu

(Image credit: Sloclap)Capcom's God Hand is one of my favourite PS2 games. It was a true cult classic, riffing on Fist of the North Star with ludicrous cutscenes, but having one of the best third-person combat systems ever (and getting an infamous IGN 3/10 review for its trouble). There aren't many games that have been able to capture the physicality of its hand-to-hand brawls or customisable combos, but developer Sloclap has specifically called the game out as an influence on 2022's wonderfully brutal Sifu (75% off $10/£8). It's tonally a far more serious proposition, but its enthralling and beautifully animated fistfights did reawaken my God Hand muscle memory.

Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

(Image credit: Capcom)Outside of its well-known franchises, Capcom made a lot of random stuff for the PS2, like Chaos Legion, Auto Modellista, Gregory Horror Show and Clock Tower 3 (if you know what all of those games are, we are the same person). Kunitsu-Gami (25% off at £30/£25) feels like a lost stablemate to those: you recruit villagers to help you defend against hordes of demons that come at night, which are dead set on attacking the maiden you're charged with protecting. You also have a suite of hack-and-slash abilities to use, so it's an inventive hybrid of action and strategy. While there's no way it would've looked this handsome as a PS2 game, it's exactly the sort of thing you'd have expected from the publisher behind Killer7 and P.N.03. We gave it 86%.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33

(Image credit: Sandfall Interactive)"Oh, these guys really like Final Fantasy 10," I thought when I first played Expedition 33 (20% off at $40/£34). To be fair, you feel it more in the world-building and story than the actual bones of its turn-based combat, which feel more like they're drawn from Lost Odyssey on Xbox 360 and Sekiro. The world-ending threat is so similar in Clair Obscur and FF10: the Paintress erases adults of a certain age on an endless cycle, and Final Fantasy 10's giant destructive whale Sin always comes back even if it's destroyed. The melancholy denizens trying to get on with life in a doomed but beautiful world is something crucial that the games have in common, too.

And now, some actual PS2 games

Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater

(Image credit: Konami)A few years ago, you couldn't even play MGS3 on PC without an emulator—and now you have two decent ways to play it. The original version comes in the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 1 (50% off at $30/£25). Delta, the remake, is also 30% off. Take your pick, but I personally think the PS2 aesthetic holds up. MGS3 was the less hyped of the two PS2 Metal Gears, mostly because Sons of Liberty was used as an early tech showcase for the platform. But Snake Eater is a more complete game with superior boss battles and the best story in the series.

Final Fantasy 10/10-2 HD Remaster

(Image credit: Square Enix)RPG purists may argue Final Fantasy 12 is a better game—it certainly has stronger localisation and voice acting, and aims for mature storytelling over anime nonsense. It's the easy-to-parse combat and progression systems that keep me coming back to Final Fantasy 10 (60% off at $12/£8), not to mention how distinctive the world of Spira is. The soundtrack is loaded with bops, and might be the part of the game that's endured the most for me. If you like PS2-era Japanese RPGs, you're actually spoiled for choice on Steam: Phantom Brave, Tales of Symphonia, Grandia 2, Kingdom Hearts (if you don't mind stretching the definition) and more are also on sale.

Rez Infinite

(Image credit: Enhance)I always think of Rez as a Dreamcast-first game, but it was actually released simultaneously in Japan on both PS2 and Sega's final console. Still, it feels Sega to its core. This Panzer Dragoon-style rhythm shooter where you're fighting evil viruses in a computer network has a beautiful Y2K aesthetic, and Rez Infinite (70% off at $8/£6) brought it to modern platforms with a well-received expansion to the original game. It's not a long experience, so the price here is spot-on.

Shin Megami Tensei 3 Nocturne HD Remaster

(Image credit: Atlus)It goes without saying that Persona 3 Reload and Persona 4 Golden are easy recommendations from the Atlus RPG stable, since both games started their lives on PS2. Persona 4 Revival seems like it'll keep to the same standard, too. The publisher's other games were always a bit weirder and more impenetrable, though, like Nocturne (70% off at $15/£13), an atmospheric and hardcore monster battling game from the mainline Shin Megami Tensei series. Known as Lucifer's Call in the UK, it was my first exposure to Atlus. I never finished it and lost my save when my launch model PS3 died, but 20 years after I first played Nocturne, the specific dour feeling of its post-apocalyptic Tokyo still sticks in my memory. An acquired taste, but the people who love this game really love it.

Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny

(Image credit: Capcom)"I wonder what PC Gamer gave one of my favourite games of all time," I asked myself this morning. Turns out the answer was 65%. Oof! I love Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny (50% off at $15/£12.49), because it offers a branching path at numerous points in the story based on how friendly you are with the four different warrior companions in the game. Samurai's Destiny is at the midpoint between old school Resident Evil's fixed camera survival horror and Devil May Cry's hack-and-slash combat (except more methodical and less acrobatic). A great Steam Deck game, as you might expect.

Welcome to LOST WEEKEND, VICE’s Monday briefing.

Forget about curing cancer and ending war; what I really need from AI is it to get me a ticket for the Glastonbury Festival.

If I had my way, Glastonbury would become a gathering of the 210,000 most effective users of agentic AI in the world. The hippies and hedonists who’ve hogged it for the last however many decades have had their turn. Newsflash, wastoids: There are plenty of other parties where you can torch your brain cells and pump your biological age up a full generational bracket. Surely what I’m saying isn’t even that controversial. The true spirit of Glastonbury is transformation. And what could be more transformative for Western Europe than its very own Burning Man?

The second- and third-order benefits are difficult to compute. In my brave new world, Glasto would simply be attended by a better quality of person, the whole thing undergoing a kind of demographic transfusion: partygoers out, go-getters in. What, you thought us AI guys would be handing over our entrepreneurial smarts at the gate? Before you know it, we’ll be monetizing the portaloos, converting human waste into revenue for the suits in charge. We’ll be bussing in blood boys to turn the VIP into a hangover-free zone. The chat at sunrise will be like nothing the Stone Circle has ever heard before, as tech-bro visionaries debate the merits of psychedelic drugs and whether or not we’re living in a simulation.


“Before you know it, we’ll be monetizing the portaloos, converting human waste into revenue for the suits in charge”


No doubt there will be naysayers. The usual suspects will complain that entry to Glastonbury should be determined by how much each potential consumer actually cares about music (yawn). But this would result in the most suboptimal festival in living memory, with disparate clusters of black metal connoisseurs and Japanese noise aficionados stumbling across the 600-hectare site, blinking like trapped moles. Some folks are just better off in their bedrooms.

I don’t know why people are crying about the price of tickets, which are just £408, or to put it another way, less than an annual subscription to GPT Plus. Fortunately, there is little need to worry about depressing brokies these days, after security tightened up around the turn of the century, cutting off the kind of audacious freeloaders who loved music so much they were prepared to pole-vault a moat of human excrement to listen to some.

Increasingly, the tides are shifting in our direction. Putting tickets for the world’s biggest festival on sale at 9AM on a Sunday felt like a message to the pill-poppers and freakniks that they’re no longer welcome; no doubt most of them were too busy sleeping off their hangovers to log into a platoon of devices and stare at a set of unmoving green bars for four hours. Even if the queue contained the odd degenerate who’d been awake all night, I’m confident they couldn’t have successfully navigated a purchase that didn’t involve at least one Albanian man. Which is great, as these are the last people you’d actually want to hang out with at a festival.


Simon Reynolds on ‘Heroin’, Rock’s Most Evil Song


Since the introduction of ID verification, buying tickets for Glastonbury has been a test of how effectively you can organize friends and family members into your very own home bot-farm operation. AI puts an end to that. There will be no more screaming at grandmother because her arthritic fingers can’t enter the registration numbers fast enough to complete a purchase on her Kindle’s internet browser. AI can do that job way better, then book flights to Ghent so we can euthanize her.

There was a last-minute change to the system this year, but it was easy enough to get around. The new “hack” was to gather up as many unused registrations as possible—begging, bribing, or blackmailing anyone who’s had kids or got sober since the last instalment of the festival in 2025—and making use of the extra unique queue numbers. I can neither confirm nor deny the existence of an underground trade in the registration numbers of the recently deceased. Did you know they eat their fries with mayonnaise in Belgium?


“I don’t know why people are crying about the price of tickets, which are just £408, or to put it another way, less than an annual subscription to GPT Plus”


I learned that this week. AI agents are already making dinner reservations. Once they work out how to get into Glastonbury, you’ll know the singularity isn’t far away. AI can refresh a browser window faster than any human in history, so hopefully next year, the ticket rush will be a thing of the past. And if you drugged-out doomers don’t like the sound of that, you can stay home and watch on the BBC—as long as your agent has sorted out the license renewal.

OTHER NEWS


Shout out to Kid Rock collaborating with Eminem for some religious rap about staying friends despite having political differences. Gonna be one of my least favorite genres.

FBI Director Kash Patel just got engaged to country singer Alexis Wilkins, which implies the existence of unfathomably hideous his-and-hers customized Nikes (good luck finding a wedding dress to go with them).

London’s underground art fair, Minor Attractions, returns this month and will include live music for the first time—one of the venues is the kinky co-working space STÜCK (which we’ve written about before), which I guess makes sense as it’s a pretty… fluid space.


PREDICTION FOR THE WEEK AHEAD


After the release of single “Patient Zero”—which tragically coincided with the death of a scientist at a Russian plague laboratory—Taylor Swift’s new track, “Mass Extinction Event”, is an unexpected return to form (streaming numbers are down though after millions die from Black Death 2.0).


BRAND NEW SENTENCE


“The two-year-old robots were trained to throw themselves into molten steel after no longer serving a purpose”

items.title: Viral AI-Generated Comedian Steals Jokes And Is Rewarded With Millions Of Views
items.author: Zack Zwiezen
items.summary: Shorts created with generative AI tools have been flooding social media and vertical video platforms for a bit now. But a new example shows just how shitty
items.text:
Shorts created with generative AI tools have been flooding social media and vertical video platforms for a bit now. But a new example shows just how shitty things can be, as a stand-up comedian alleged that someone had used AI tools to rip off his joke using a fake AI-slop woman who is becoming quite popular on Instagram.

Tiffany Sloan is the name given to an AI-generated character that appears in numerous AI-slop Instagram Reels, often featuring her telling a joke in front of a fake audience. Some of these videos are very popular, with one stand-up clip hitting over 7 million views in just under two weeks. Here’s that video, which is a pretty good example of 90 percent of the content posted on the Sloan account.

Sloan’s creator is unknown, but what we do know is that this AI slop character has been gaining followers quickly on Meta’s social media platform. Since the account started posting on September 11, barely three weeks ago, it’s already garnered over 375,000 followers. Also, in that short amount of time, Sloan has posted 75 videos, most of which feature the AI character telling a joke. The problem is, some are claiming Sloan’s creator is stealing those jokes.

On October 3, comedian George Brett Olson shared a video comparing one of Sloan’s jokes to an excerpt from his own performance, and it’s clear that someone was, at the very least, inspired by not only Olson’s joke, but his outfit, too.

And not only is the Sloan account allegedly ripping off jokes, with Olson claiming that other comedians are having their jokes stolen as well, but the account is also monetizing all of the views and engagement it earns using this method of AI-powered joke theft. Olson also claims that someone, possibly the same person running the Sloan account, is stealing many of the same jokes but using different AI-generated women of various races. And all of this is because this is how the internet works now, thanks to companies like Meta.

Engagement is the main way to make money, and the bigger your numbers, the more money you can make. And with AI-generation tools, it’s now easier than ever for one person to flood multiple accounts with slop starring pretty women or weird people and make a ton of money in the process. In fact, thanks to the power of AI, Sloan can appear in clips with famous actors like Kaley Cuoco and Danny DeVito. And the creator behind Sloan can easily whip up a few variants of the same joke using different clothing and actors to see which one the algorithm rewards more. And if you really, really like Sloan, “she” even has an OnlyFans account.

This is our future, and it sucks. And we can blame it entirely on big tech companies not only making generative-AI tech but then creating structures that incentivize and financially reward people who use these same tools to flood the internet with stuff. What kind of stuff? Doesn’t matter, really. All that matters is that people click and watch. Maybe comment. If they do, the creator is rewarded and makes more content like that to feed the machine.

The future is going to be millions of these AI videos flooding every corner of your digital life, and the only thing that will break them up will be the gambling app ads starring famous actors and sports stars. And people like Mark Zuckerberg will be even richer by then, so at least someone is benefiting from all this slop and enshittifcation.

items.author: Saloni Gajjar

items.text:
At one point in CBS’s Cupertino, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller) exasperatedly asks, “Is anybody not paranoid?” Christy, an assistant at an upstart law firm waging a crusade against Big Tech, raises a valid question. Thanks to the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and the algorithm-driven social media that preceded it, it’s impossible not to be anxious about data mining, the surveillance state, and whether AI’s next target will be everyone’s jobs. This is paranoia that creators Robert and Michael King are tapping into for their latest primetime drama.


In Cupertino, attorneys Michael Price (Mike Colter), Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), and Natalia Boutella (Busy Philipps) team up—along with Christy, of course—to take down the billion-dollar companies that gave Silicon Valley its name. Their clients are the people who have been wronged by these digital Goliaths, with the show name-dropping the so-called Magnificent Seven—Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla—often. After helming shows like The Good Wife, The Good Fight, and Evil, the Kings return to a familiar framework with Cupertino: spinning extremely timely topics into an amusing case-of-the-week series.


Ahead of the show’s October 8 premiere, The A.V. Club spoke to Robert and Michelle King about the progression of their AI-related story, why they put humanity at the core of Cupertino, and what to expect from season one.


This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

The A.V. Club: You’ve been mulling over a version of this show since The Good Wife was wrapping up. What made you want to stick with it for a decade, and how much did the idea evolve over the past decade?


Robert King: I do think the AI boom suddenly made it more current, not less. You’re always running ideas through your mind, sometimes for years, and then there are certain things going on in the day-to-day and in the news, so you feel like this is a good way to go.


Part of our writing is therapy. Part of all this is us going, “Okay, how do we take in the Trump years in The Good Fight, how do you even deal with something like that?” Actually, the same thing happened with BrainDead, where we suddenly saw the Newt Gingrich partisanship was taking over. It was in the news constantly.


Michelle King: As we were trying to figure out a way to do this, it became a very different concept as well of a David-versus-Goliath story. That’s how we now have this law firm that attacks the Goliaths who took over Silicon Valley. It became a very enticing story for us to tell, and we fell in love with these characters.


RK: We don’t lead with the math or the algorithms. Why do that when you can lead with humans? It’s much more engaging that way. I understand this algorithm and this tech, but we’re not going to be leading with it.


AVC: As the industry itself tries to figure out where it stands on AI, I’m curious if you had any worry about placing a drama like Cupertino on TV right now?


MK: Not really because we have a home studio with CBS, so we brought it directly to them and pitched it. They embraced it immediately, and we’ve never gotten a moment of pushback from them or CBS network. We have been lucky that way.


RK: Michelle and I have a good kid, bad kid thing going on. We present ourselves as the good kids, but as soon as they let us in the door, we’re like, “Oh my God, let’s go after the NSA in The Good Wife” or something like that. You’re always looking for ways to break a little pottery.


AVC: What was the process of figuring out the stories to include in Cupertino‘s case of the week element so it stays current?


RK: Well, it’s not just both of us. It’s six other spectacular writers, five of whom we’ve worked with before on other shows going back to The Good Wife. So it was a constant back and forth in terms of ideas, articles, and culling through things we wanted to explore. The episode titles probably point to why we were engaged with the story. The title of each episode is the name of the client being defended. What we start with is the humanity, because that’s the only way to engage with such big concepts. In episode five, we have a data tasker, with a single mom, who makes $1,000 a week from doing this massive amount of tasks to teach the computers and AI of these billion and trillion dollar companies. The story doesn’t write itself, but you get why someone who is basically working day and night to teach a computer what a soft target and hard target looks like is fascinating.


AVC: What can you tease about some of the upcoming episodes, and do you have any favorites that stuck with you?


MK: Oh my God, that is really unfair, it is like choosing between your children.


RK: I will say, I know there’s an embargo on what’s coming out of the reveal at the end of episode two, but one of my favorite things, and it’s not just the subject matter, but the way we peel it away in that episode, about Rob McClure’s character. You’re always falling in love with subject matter, but when the subject matter is played by an excellent actor who moves it beyond your conception of it, it’s always the best. If I had to put a finger on it, there’s a bunker-related story which names names, is interesting, and points to these trillionaires who control our lives and it says, “Okay, this is the problem.” It’s high up on my list.


MK: I won’t say much but I do love it when they’re up in an airplane in the fourth episode.


AVC: No spoilers from me either, but I appreciated the episode featuring Method Man that digs into AI-generated music and how it affects artists.


RK: Yes! Aurin Squire wrote that episode. It’s something very close to his heart, the way the music industry is being eaten away from inside.


AVC: How did you assemble the cast for Cupertino, from reuniting with Mike Colter to the Girls5eva reunion with Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry?


MK: We were hopeful from the beginning that Mike Colter would be Michael Price. Obviously, it’s not a particularly creative choice for the character’s name on our part.


RK: It’s like Andrea Martin playing Sister Andrea on Evil, so it worked out.


MK: We’ve never worked with Rachel Keller before, but she is spectacular, as is Ella Stiller. We could not be more fortunate.


RK: And yes, we are big Girls5eva fans, and we were really sad to see that show go away. Both of us just really wanted to work with Busy, especially because of Renée Elise Goldsberry. But there are some great people overall, including new faces like Nik Dodani.


MK: Nik is another actor we’ve wanted to work with because he’s great at comedy and drama, which is what we look for every time we cast any of our shows.


AVC: Do you have any dream guest stars, considering the show’s format?


RK: We’ve always wanted John Lithgow. We wanted him on everything we’ve done, and we got so close one year on The Good Fight. He’s remarkable and a lot of fun.


MK: We can put that out in the universe. And I will add Meryl Streep.


AVC: My pitch is for another Evil reunion with Katja Herbers as an Elizabeth Holmes-style character.


RK: Oh my God, Katja. She’s filming another TV show right now, I believe, but that would be so much fun to have her play someone like that.


AVC: Is it too early to ask if you’ve thought about the show’s future or how long you envision it going on for, and whether you’ll have enough material to do it?


MK: I mean, as long as CBS will have us, I guess. I feel like there’s so much material, I almost worry about the world running out before the material.


RK: You’re always worried about overstaying your welcome, but I do think the modern TV world is more about how you get canceled instead of [choosing to end.] We were stunned by Evil being canceled. Before that we were able to put our finger on deciding, “Okay, this is our last season and we might be able plan how to end it.” With that in mind, you’re securing two very cautious showrunners who, you know, have a larger appetite than I think TV wants to give you. That’s all a bad way to put it, but I think you understand.


AVC: You’re executive producers on Elsbeth, which is part of The Good Wife universe and airs right before Cupertino. What are the chances of a crossover?


MK: I don’t think that’s going to happen in terms of a crossover.


RK: But there are some really good guest stars this year on Elsbeth. Jon Tolins, the showrunner, does a great job. They’re about four or five episodes into filming right now. Cupertino started earlier, so we’re shooting episode 17 now. What I will say about Elsbeth is there will be more interaction between Wendell Pierce and Carrie Preston’s characters. There are no two more charming actors than them. They love working with each other, and you can tell, so the most fun time watching the show is when they’re interacting.


AVC: Having done this in The Good Wife, Evil, and now Cupertino, what’s the trick to make serious, relevant topics also feel lighthearted and funny enough for a network drama? How do you toe that line as storytellers?


RK: I think some writers are lie detectors. They react to lies like it’s a curse.


For us, it’s earnestness. That’s our version of lie detectors. When we sense that something’s getting too earnest, that’s when you throw in a fart joke or suddenly you have someone have massive diarrhea. I don’t think we did that this year, but basically there’s always something human. You’ll find a lot of food and alcohol is discussed in our shows, and that’s because there’s a humanity within the massive stories. Everybody goes to the bathroom or wants a good meal or have a good time drinking.


MK: That’s exactly it. Without it, stuff becomes unwatchable. Or it can get too serious, which we see often in news stories anyway.


AVC: You’re tackling the show’s subject matter from different points of view, but are there specific takeaways you wanted the audience to have from Cupertino?


MK: We wanted to ask more questions than make a definitive point of view because, yes, the characters don’t all have the exact same point of view either. If you start making one, then you get awfully close to preachy and then already I’m reaching for the remote control.


RK: I would summarize the instinct behind it is not to lose track of humanity because I do think the show is about how everybody in Silicon Valley is obsessed with the tech. The core meaning of our law firm, but also of our show, is that people is what it should all be about. AI is kicking a lot of people out of work, and will kick out a lot more. It seems stupid because who is going to buy these services if we don’t have money. I don’t care what Elon Musk says, there is never going to be income for everyone for free, that’s insane. I do think there’s this utopian view that loses track of the here and now and what humans are and what they’re about and the brilliance of the human brain. It gets downgraded when they compare it to AI.


MK: Yeah, that’s a lovely thing to bring it down to. Don’t lose track of humanity.


Saloni Gajjar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic. You can read her review of Cupertino here, and follow her recaps of the show, which premieres October 8 at 10 p.m. ET on CBS.

blocks.x: At one point in CBS’s Cupertino, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller) exasperatedly asks, “Is anybody not paranoid?” Christy, an assistant at an upstart law firm waging a crusade against Big Tech, raises a valid question. Thanks to the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and the algorithm-driven social media that preceded it, it’s impossible not to be anxious about data mining, the surveillance state, and whether AI’s next target will be everyone’s jobs. This is paranoia that creators Robert and Michael King are tapping into for their latest primetime drama.

In Cupertino, attorneys Michael Price (Mike Colter), Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), and Natalia Boutella (Busy Philipps) team up—along with Christy, of course—to take down the billion-dollar companies that gave Silicon Valley its name. Their clients are the people who have been wronged by these digital Goliaths, with the show name-dropping the so-called Magnificent Seven—Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla—often. After helming shows like The Good Wife, The Good Fight, and Evil, the Kings return to a familiar framework with Cupertino: spinning extremely timely topics into an amusing case-of-the-week series.

Ahead of the show’s October 8 premiere, The A.V. Club spoke to Robert and Michelle King about the progression of their AI-related story, why they put humanity at the core of Cupertino, and what to expect from season one.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

The A.V. Club: You’ve been mulling over a version of this show since The Good Wife was wrapping up. What made you want to stick with it for a decade, and how much did the idea evolve over the past decade?

Robert King: I do think the AI boom suddenly made it more current, not less. You’re always running ideas through your mind, sometimes for years, and then there are certain things going on in the day-to-day and in the news, so you feel like this is a good way to go.

Part of our writing is therapy. Part of all this is us going, “Okay, how do we take in the Trump years in The Good Fight, how do you even deal with something like that?” Actually, the same thing happened with BrainDead, where we suddenly saw the Newt Gingrich partisanship was taking over. It was in the news constantly.

Michelle King: As we were trying to figure out a way to do this, it became a very different concept as well of a David-versus-Goliath story. That’s how we now have this law firm that attacks the Goliaths who took over Silicon Valley. It became a very enticing story for us to tell, and we fell in love with these characters.

RK: We don’t lead with the math or the algorithms. Why do that when you can lead with humans? It’s much more engaging that way. I understand this algorithm and this tech, but we’re not going to be leading with it.
AVC: As the industry itself tries to figure out where it stands on AI, I’m curious if you had any worry about placing a drama like Cupertino on TV right now?

MK: Not really because we have a home studio with CBS, so we brought it directly to them and pitched it. They embraced it immediately, and we’ve never gotten a moment of pushback from them or CBS network. We have been lucky that way.

RK: Michelle and I have a good kid, bad kid thing going on. We present ourselves as the good kids, but as soon as they let us in the door, we’re like, “Oh my God, let’s go after the NSA in The Good Wife” or something like that. You’re always looking for ways to break a little pottery.
AVC: What was the process of figuring out the stories to include in Cupertino‘s case of the week element so it stays current?

RK: Well, it’s not just both of us. It’s six other spectacular writers, five of whom we’ve worked with before on other shows going back to The Good Wife. So it was a constant back and forth in terms of ideas, articles, and culling through things we wanted to explore. The episode titles probably point to why we were engaged with the story. The title of each episode is the name of the client being defended. What we start with is the humanity, because that’s the only way to engage with such big concepts. In episode five, we have a data tasker, with a single mom, who makes $1,000 a week from doing this massive amount of tasks to teach the computers and AI of these billion and trillion dollar companies. The story doesn’t write itself, but you get why someone who is basically working day and night to teach a computer what a soft target and hard target looks like is fascinating.
AVC: What can you tease about some of the upcoming episodes, and do you have any favorites that stuck with you?
MK: Oh my God, that is really unfair, it is like choosing between your children.

RK: I will say, I know there’s an embargo on what’s coming out of the reveal at the end of episode two, but one of my favorite things, and it’s not just the subject matter, but the way we peel it away in that episode, about Rob McClure’s character. You’re always falling in love with subject matter, but when the subject matter is played by an excellent actor who moves it beyond your conception of it, it’s always the best. If I had to put a finger on it, there’s a bunker-related story which names names, is interesting, and points to these trillionaires who control our lives and it says, “Okay, this is the problem.” It’s high up on my list.
MK: I won’t say much but I do love it when they’re up in an airplane in the fourth episode.
AVC: No spoilers from me either, but I appreciated the episode featuring Method Man that digs into AI-generated music and how it affects artists.
RK: Yes! Aurin Squire wrote that episode. It’s something very close to his heart, the way the music industry is being eaten away from inside.
AVC: How did you assemble the cast for Cupertino, from reuniting with Mike Colter to the Girls5eva reunion with Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry?
MK: We were hopeful from the beginning that Mike Colter would be Michael Price. Obviously, it’s not a particularly creative choice for the character’s name on our part.
RK: It’s like Andrea Martin playing Sister Andrea on Evil, so it worked out.
MK: We’ve never worked with Rachel Keller before, but she is spectacular, as is Ella Stiller. We could not be more fortunate.

RK: And yes, we are big Girls5eva fans, and we were really sad to see that show go away. Both of us just really wanted to work with Busy, especially because of Renée Elise Goldsberry. But there are some great people overall, including new faces like Nik Dodani.
MK: Nik is another actor we’ve wanted to work with because he’s great at comedy and drama, which is what we look for every time we cast any of our shows.
AVC: Do you have any dream guest stars, considering the show’s format?
RK: We’ve always wanted John Lithgow. We wanted him on everything we’ve done, and we got so close one year on The Good Fight. He’s remarkable and a lot of fun.
MK: We can put that out in the universe. And I will add Meryl Streep.
AVC: My pitch is for another Evil reunion with Katja Herbers as an Elizabeth Holmes-style character.
RK: Oh my God, Katja. She’s filming another TV show right now, I believe, but that would be so much fun to have her play someone like that.
AVC: Is it too early to ask if you’ve thought about the show’s future or how long you envision it going on for, and whether you’ll have enough material to do it?
MK: I mean, as long as CBS will have us, I guess. I feel like there’s so much material, I almost worry about the world running out before the material.

RK: You’re always worried about overstaying your welcome, but I do think the modern TV world is more about how you get canceled instead of [choosing to end.] We were stunned by Evil being canceled. Before that we were able to put our finger on deciding, “Okay, this is our last season and we might be able plan how to end it.” With that in mind, you’re securing two very cautious showrunners who, you know, have a larger appetite than I think TV wants to give you. That’s all a bad way to put it, but I think you understand.
AVC: You’re executive producers on Elsbeth, which is part of The Good Wife universe and airs right before Cupertino. What are the chances of a crossover?
MK: I don’t think that’s going to happen in terms of a crossover.

RK: But there are some really good guest stars this year on Elsbeth. Jon Tolins, the showrunner, does a great job. They’re about four or five episodes into filming right now. Cupertino started earlier, so we’re shooting episode 17 now. What I will say about Elsbeth is there will be more interaction between Wendell Pierce and Carrie Preston’s characters. There are no two more charming actors than them. They love working with each other, and you can tell, so the most fun time watching the show is when they’re interacting.

AVC: Having done this in The Good Wife, Evil, and now Cupertino, what’s the trick to make serious, relevant topics also feel lighthearted and funny enough for a network drama? How do you toe that line as storytellers?
RK: I think some writers are lie detectors. They react to lies like it’s a curse.

For us, it’s earnestness. That’s our version of lie detectors. When we sense that something’s getting too earnest, that’s when you throw in a fart joke or suddenly you have someone have massive diarrhea. I don’t think we did that this year, but basically there’s always something human. You’ll find a lot of food and alcohol is discussed in our shows, and that’s because there’s a humanity within the massive stories. Everybody goes to the bathroom or wants a good meal or have a good time drinking.
MK: That’s exactly it. Without it, stuff becomes unwatchable. Or it can get too serious, which we see often in news stories anyway.
AVC: You’re tackling the show’s subject matter from different points of view, but are there specific takeaways you wanted the audience to have from Cupertino?

MK: We wanted to ask more questions than make a definitive point of view because, yes, the characters don’t all have the exact same point of view either. If you start making one, then you get awfully close to preachy and then already I’m reaching for the remote control.

RK: I would summarize the instinct behind it is not to lose track of humanity because I do think the show is about how everybody in Silicon Valley is obsessed with the tech. The core meaning of our law firm, but also of our show, is that people is what it should all be about. AI is kicking a lot of people out of work, and will kick out a lot more. It seems stupid because who is going to buy these services if we don’t have money. I don’t care what Elon Musk says, there is never going to be income for everyone for free, that’s insane. I do think there’s this utopian view that loses track of the here and now and what humans are and what they’re about and the brilliance of the human brain. It gets downgraded when they compare it to AI.
MK: Yeah, that’s a lovely thing to bring it down to. Don’t lose track of humanity.

items.text:
In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right.

The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar.

In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind.

Watch on YouTube

RetroSpace takes place aboard Aurora 5, a pseudo-1970s interstellar ark that has tumbled into a black hole, and somehow come away with a mild case of temporal indecision – certain areas flip between timeframes - rather than spaghettification and incomprehensible doom. You are a janitor, woken from cryo to find a lot of stuff on fire, a lot of people dead, and a lot of other people deranged and monsterfied by gene-modding. Taking up your power wrench, you set out for the habitat hub and soon become embroiled in missions assigned by a handful of coherent survivors, including a sentient AI and a talking pig fellah.

These take you out to the far corners of the space station, which is very much the main character here. There's a "garden" sector that consists of a verdant silo with a starry dome, its spiral stairs and crawlspaces leading down to what I think is a bubbling soup of fertiliser. There's a train that circles the whole facility – not a camouflaged loading screen, as with chapter breaks in Dead Space, but an actual monorail car that travels in real time. There are a lot of audiologs, hackable terminals, and comedy public safety signs or adverts. As you might expect from the devisers of chicken detective games, RetroSpace skews toward caricature, which can get obnoxious – there's an audiolog early on that pokes fun at NPCs who leave scary audiologs. Still, it feels like the devs are fundamentally committed to making an engrossing world.

There's a persistent mystique woven around the station's janitors. Propaganda posters cast you and your lost brethren as urban legends, seldom seen by regular folk because you're always up a ladder or behind a bulkhead doing whatever it is you helmeted weirdos do with those sprays and spanners. Each sector has a locked or concealed utility closet with a portal to the Janitor's Haven - an interdimensional hideaway set up by union organisers, where you'll hang out with story-critical NPCs and do the bulk of your upgrading and customising.

If the station is a peach, I'm a little less convinced so far by the tools at your disposal. On the one hand, you've got weapons such as pistols, shotguns, and rayguns, all (eventually) upgradeable. On the other, you've got more indirect or tactical accessories such as cloaking devices, computer-hacking gizmos, and propulsive fire extinguishers. On the third hand, you've got genetic engineering or Mutamods, which range from giving yourself grasshopper thighs for higher jumping, moth ears so that you heal in light, or biceps full of rhino DNA for meatier clobbering.

The gene-modding cuts both ways: when you die, you'll be cloned for free at the nearest Bacta tank equivalent, but you'll be saddled with a random cartoon affliction for your troubles. I came away from one misadventure with a body prone to uncontrollable sneezing and swearing, which did not help with subsequent attempts at stealth. Fortunately, you can purge the debuffs by siphoning genetic material from the nearest vanilla human corpse, and Aurora 5 has no shortage of those.

Within the world, you can also do things like hold up crates to block bullets, or spray paths of water to create an electricity trap before smacking a circuit box. It's all entertaining enough, but many of the ideas are overly familiar from System Shock, Bioshock and Arkane's Prey. I'm really hoping that somewhere in RetroSpace, there lurks a tool or combination of tools that is as daft in its own way as Prey's Mimic ability. Or the slapstick bullshit you get in Skin Deep.

As it is, I'm finding that I'm too often just shooting enemies because I'm unexcited by the more devious ways of avoiding or defeating them. The enemies have their moments – lop a bugman's head off, and it might sprout legs, while the manpigs are drawn to trails of blood - but a lot of the time, they're just awareness indicators you can either avoid or gun down.

If you're comfortable with how comfortable RetroSpace can feel, as a love letter to certain famous immersive sims, you'll likely be able to forgive all this. Myself, I'd say the station ambience and secretive level design are worth the occasional sense of deja-vu. I'll keep plugging on with the game, though games journalism being what it currently is, I sadly don't have time for a full review. Find out more about RetroSpace on Steam. Let me know if you spot any really sexy airvents.

items.text:
Updated
Oct 6, 2026, 4:58 AM EDT

Writing from the Chicagoland area in Illinois, Robert is an avid movie watcher and will take just about any excuse to find time to go to his local movie theaters. Robert graduated from Bradley University with degrees in Journalism and Game Design with a minor in Film Studies. Robert tries his best to keep up with all the latest movie releases, from those released in theaters to those released on streaming. While he doesn't always keep up with the latest TV shows, he makes it a goal to watch nearly every major new release possible. He has been honing his craft and following any and all movie news all his life, leading up to now, where he has a vast knowledge of film and film history. He also logs every movie that he watches on his Letterboxd page, and has hosted a weekly online movie night with his closest friends for over 6 years.

While they seem like complete opposites, rarely have two different genres complemented and worked so well together as horror and comedy. The harsh contrast between gore, violence, and scares and silly, non-serious comedy has made for a collection of highly memorable and iconic experiences over the years. Ranging from massive blockbuster hits like Zombieland and Gremlins to certified cult classics like Evil Dead and Jennifer's Body, the combination is a fan favorite among audiences.

The 2020s have been no stranger to exceptional horror comedy experiences, playing into the latest trends and conventions of horror filmmaking and modern humor. Horror comedy is arguably at the height of its popularity and capabilities, with exciting new and creative films in the genre released throughout the year to audience acclaim. Indeed, these are the best horror comedies from the 2020s so far, proving that a film can make viewers scream in fear and laughter alike.

25
'Y2K' (2024)

Image via A24

A wildly entertaining apocalyptic horror comedy as well as a brazen blast to the past and reexamination of the goofy trends and culture of the late '90s, Y2K gets a lot of mileage out of the inherent fun of its premise. The film takes place in an alternate version of New Year's Eve, 1999, where the fabled Y2K bug rumor ends up coming true, plunging the world into a chaotic, technology-caused apocalypse. As a dangerous virus begins harvesting humanity for their brainpower, it becomes up to a ragtag group of teens to save their lives as well as the entire world.

While more subdued and character-driven than many other horror comedies of the 2020s, Y2K's distinct flavor of comedy and absurdist wit helps it stand out with an array of memorable scenes and standout moments. It acts as a massive love letter to the '90s as a whole, embracing the stark difference that 25 years can make in culture as it stars a wide cast of teens who weren't even alive during the decade.

24
'Totally Killer' (2023)

Image via Blumhouse

Combining a classic slasher with a time-travel story, Totally Killer sees the notorious "Sweet Sixteen Killer" returning to take his revenge upon a small suburban town 35 years after his first murder spree. To discover the identity of the killer, 17-year-old Jamie (Kiernan Shipka) accidentally travels back in time to 1987, right before the first killing spree took place. With a newfound determination, Jamie is determined to hunt down and stop the killer despite the culture shock of now being in the '80s.

Time travel stories have always been rife with comedic potential, and combining this premise with the inherent charm and energy of a classic '80s slasher makes for a match made in heaven. Totally Killer is tongue-in-cheek, not only in its commentary and reflection on society's evolution in the past 35 years but also in the conventions and tropes of '80s slashers as a whole. It all comes together to make an experience that does justice to the classic slashers that it's a love letter to.

23
'Ready or Not 2: Here I Come' (2026)

Image via Searchlight Pictures

The original Ready or Not was one of the biggest pleasant surprise horror comedies of the 2010s, largely launching the careers of Radio Silence and finding great strength with its memorable characters and over-the-top bloodshed. The sequel largely continues this streak of horror comedy excellence, as Ready or Not 2: Here I Come features more wild characters, more ruthless violence, and a lot of the same sickly dark humor that made the original a hit.

The biggest draw of this sequel over the original is the addition of Kathryn Newton as sister Faith McCaullay, with her inherent chemistry and sisterly dynamic with Samara Weaving's Grace acting as the biggest strength of the film. Ready or Not 2 is also home to a lot of incredibly memorable sequences, including a hilarious pepper-spray-blinded fight scene and yet another iconic finale full of blood explosions. It certainly lives up to the reputation and fun factor of the original runaway hit, showing the growth Radio Silence has had since their breakout film.

22
'Willy's Wonderland' (2021)

Image via Screen Media Films

Easily one of Nicolas Cage's most underrated films, Willy's Wonderland sees him as a quiet and stoic man who, after having his car break down, agrees to work off the repair costs by cleaning an abandoned family fun center. However, the job is far from as simple, as he is forced to face a crew of deadly, haunted animatronics that roam the building at night with a thirst for bloodshed. As he fights and takes down the animatronics night after night, a group of teens ends up breaking into the building at the same time in search of answers.

While the film takes clear inspiration from the trend of haunted, killer animatronics popularized by the Five Nights at Freddy's video games, Willy's Wonderland certainly takes a more comedic and over-the-top approach to the premise. From Cage's hilarious non-speaking performance to the chaotic and absurd designs and hilarious action sequences, it makes for a much more comedic experience than the actual Five Nights at Freddy's movie.

21
'Hell of a Summer' (2025)

Image via Neon

Taking inspiration from classic slashers of old while adding its own signature Gen Z flair to its execution, Hell of a Summer is a simple yet incredibly approachable slasher comedy that embraces the fun and absurdity of the summer camp horror film. The film plays out like many of the summer camp horror films that inspired it, following a mysterious masked killer laying waste to various teenage camp counselors, forcing them to turn on each other as bodies begin to pile up.

What the film may be lacking in originality, it massively makes up for in terms of charm and an electrifyingly fun time, with the chemistry and antics of the cast largely being felt while watching the film. Especially for younger viewers who may not be as acclimated to the world of horror, Hell of a Summer is a great, light starting point for the genre that exudes charm and good vibes with each scene. It's a fun modernization of classic trends, tailor-made for the modern audience who hasn't seen these trends capitalized on in a long time.

20
'Abigail' (2024)

Image via Universal Pictures

One of many exceptional horror-comedy efforts from Radio Silence, Abigail sees a group of criminals tasked with kidnapping a young ballerina girl in order to obtain a ransom from her deadly gang leader father. However, as the night goes on, it becomes increasingly apparent that this is far from just an ordinary young girl, but instead a bloodthirsty vampire who sees them as her latest prey. The night soon becomes one of survival as they are forced to find any way to take down the vampire threat before they end up being killed in the process.

Abigail has a very tongue-in-cheek tone as it relishes and amplifies the fun to be had from a killer vampire girl premise, brought together by exceptional performances not just from Alisha Weir as the titular Abigail, but the entire squad of criminals. Instead of simply letting the comedy of a killer little girl do all the work, however, the film finds a great deal of comedy from other avenues, whether it be chemistry between the main cast or building off of the intricacies of Abigail as a villain.

19
'Werewolves Within' (2021)

Image via IFC Films

Adapting an extremely obscure VR video game into a werewolf whodunit film, Werewolves Within was largely given free rein to tell its own wild murder mystery film since the original game didn't really have a big story to latch onto. However, this incredibly underrated video game adaptation does a perfect job of recapturing the manic energy and chaos of a social deduction mystery game, with everyone pointing fingers at one another while the killer is hidden in plain sight.

Directed by CollegeHumor alum Josh Ruben, Werewolves Within is absolutely killer in terms of its comedic timing and depth, being incredibly self-aware of the strengths of horror comedy and murder mysteries as a whole. The film deserves a hell of a lot more appreciation and love in the horror comedy space, with its overwhelming charm and passion going a long way in terms of making it easily one of the most underrated and overlooked horror comedies of the 2020s so far.

18
'Renfield' (2023)

Image via Universal Pictures

Another hilarious horror comedy with Nicolas Cage in a primary role, Renfield brings the classic characters of Renfield (Nicholas Hoult) and Dracula (Cage) to the modern era. Growing tired and annoyed with his life of indentured servitude under the prince of darkness, Renfield begins to reevaluate and finds a path to redemption away from the clutches of Dracula. It doesn't take long before Dracula catches on to Renfield's schemes, however, placing him in danger and unleashing Dracula and his darkness upon the world.

items.text:
Steam's New Free 9/10 Stealth Game Has Serious Metal Gear Solid Vibes

Published Oct 6, 2026, 3:02 AM EDT

Sharmila is an engineer-turned-gaming hardware journalist and freelance contributor at ScreenRant who has been covering the gaming and tech industry since 2021. While she first built her expertise writing about video games, she has since pivoted towards gaming hardware, with a focus on PC components, peripherals, handhelds, and performance-driven tech. When she’s not testing gear or writing about the latest hardware trends, she can usually be found diving into competitive shooters or keeping up with the evolving esports scene.

There’s something very satisfying (and fun) about watching a guard walk past you without realizing you were standing just a few feet away. If that’s the kind of stealth you love in your video games, Steam has a new experience you’d want to check out right now.

Intravenous 3: Borderline, a free standalone prologue to the upcoming Intravenous 3, already has players comparing its stealth-heavy gameplay to games like Metal Gear Solid V—and for good reason. The best part, however, is that you can play it without having to commit to a price tag. The prologue launched on October 2, giving players a chance to experience a trailer of what the developers have been working on with Intravenous 3.

For some context about the plot, Borderline puts you in control of Gideon, a mercenary who barely survived his previous confrontation with Steve. After being hired to protect a corrupt politician, Gideon is left with very little after everything falls apart. Now, he has a trail leading back to the people responsible and a pretty straightforward reason to follow it: revenge. This setup plays out across two full missions in Borderline, which serve as an introduction to Gideon’s story and the direction Intravenous 3 is taking.

Similarities to Metal Gear become prominent in the ways you’re expected to approach each situation. Intravenous has always been built around stealth, but it isn’t the kind of game where hiding behind a wall automatically solves everything. You have to pay attention to guards, think about your positioning, and decide when it’s worth taking someone out. And, just like Metal Gear Solid V, things can get messy very quickly when your plan falls apart.

It's worth noting that Intravenous 3: Borderline, despite being just a prologue, is much more punishing than the Metal Gear experience. One mistake can turn a carefully planned infiltration into a desperate scramble for survival. So, the stealth naturally feels more deliberate. Instead of simply sneaking around because the game tells you to, you’d be doing it to avoid getting caught and facing serious consequences.

The original Intravenous game was already described by its developers as a stealth game but also a tactical hardcore gunplay for players who don’t want to find a quiet way in. Borderline carries the same vibe, where stealth and combat are closely tied together. Interestingly, that’s also part of what made Metal Gear Solid V so enjoyable. Its missions gave players plenty of room to decide how they wanted to deal with enemy positions, whether that meant carefully sneaking through or improvising when everything inevitably went wrong.

Then again, Borderline obviously isn’t trying to recreate The Phantom Pain on a smaller budget, and you shouldn’t expect an enormous open world or dozens of hours of content. This is a compact prologue designed to give you a taste of what’s coming. It's free, it's built around tactical stealth, and it gives you two proper missions rather than throwing a tiny demo at you and calling it a day.

If you’ve been missing that feeling of studying an enemy position, figuring out a route, and hoping your plan survives contact with the first guard, Intravenous 3: Borderline deserves a spot on your Steam library. And considering you don’t have to pay anything to find out whether the Metal Gear comparisons are justified, there’s really no reason not to give it a shot.

items.text:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 12:18 AM EDT

Daniel is a 27-year-old List Writer for Collider living in the south suburbs of Chicago, Illinois. As an avid film buff, he watches and analyzes many films and TV shows, especially in the horror genre, and regularly attends movie screenings.

Science fiction is the realm of endless creativity. It's the genre that has greatly influenced popular culture, delivering some of our most exciting stories and forever pushing the limits of storytelling to the absolute extremes. Sci-fi fascinated us long before the age of filmmaking really launched its popularity into the stratosphere.

We've been blessed over the last few centuries with compelling sci-fi literature. The greatest, most influential, and inspiring of these iconic novels from this genre have gone on to have a commanding presence in storytelling and even in cinema. There are notable classics that are essential, timeless even, and deserve all the praise we give them. From a beloved intergalactic adventure comedy to one of the most powerful space epics of all time, these are essential sci-fi books you need to read at least once.

'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy' (1979)

Image via Crown

Starting off is The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, a beloved sci-fi comedy novel based on a radio series of the same name by Douglas Adams. A hilarious adventure spanning multiple unique worlds, it's a delightful blast that devoted sci-fi lovers have enjoyed for nearly half a century now. It follows the misadventures of Arthur Dent, the last man alive after Earth's cataclysmic destruction, as he goes exploring the most absurd reaches of outer space with his alien best friend Ford Perfect.

Upon publication, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy became an instant sci-fi classic, one that readers loved so much that it spawned an equally successful book series and even a cult favorite film adaptation in 2005 starring Martin Freeman as Dent. It blends uproarious comedy with thrilling sci-fi adventures, culminating in an endlessly fun story that's worth reading from front to back.

'Who Goes There?' (1938)

Image via Gateway

Written by one of the most influential science fiction authors to ever live, John W. Campbell, comes the groundbreaking novella Who Goes There?, a masterclass in storytelling. This 1938 classic revolutionized the sci-fi horror genre, popularizing it with its frighteningly creative tale that perfectly balanced the two. It tells of an American research team under attack in their isolated outpost in Antarctica by a menacing shapeshifting alien organism that is able to disguise itself as any of them.

It's nearly 230 pages of perfect suspense and terror, creating an uneasy reading experience. Not to mention, it hits the ground running in its first ten pages, gripping readers immediately with its great character introductions, and it subtly teases what horrors await them later in the story. It not only influenced the genre in literature, it also impacted cinema as well, as its two notable film adaptations, 1954's The Thing From Another World and John Carpenter's 1982 classic The Thing, became dominant forces in pop culture, even becoming recognized as some of the best horror movies ever created. Overall, Campbell's novel is a trailblazer that sci-fi fans can truly appreciate.

'Neuromancer' (1984)

Image via Ace Books

An icon of the sci-fi genre that birthed the modern cyberpunk aesthetic, author William Gibson's 1984 award-winning novel Neuromancer is a staple that any sci-fi enthusiast has at least heard about. A kick-ass tale full of high-stakes action, heist-adventure excitement, and AI rampant mayhem, it follows a skilled but disgraced hacker named Case as he's recruited to help merge two very powerful artificial entities into a super-intelligence.

Neuromancer is a striking novel with excellently explored themes about corporate supremacy, identity and body loss, and moral uncertainty advancing artifical intelligence. In short, it's an essential read that has remained consistently popular since its publication. It not only revolutionized the cyberpunk look and defined it for decades, but also became a benchmark for other A.I. related thrillers, cementing itself as a timelessly inspired masterpiece.

'1984' (1949)

Image via Penguin Books

One of the eeriest sci-fi dystopian groundbreakers of all time, George Orwell's 1984 has kept readers paranoid for decades. It's a revolutionary tale that brought thought-provoking themes of totalitarianism and suppression to the frightening realm of possibility. The story is set in an alternate future where an endless war devastating the planet has caused Great Britain to form a totalitarian state, causing a dictatorial leader, Big Brother, to rule with an iron fist. In the wake of the government's complete control over everyone, one man, Winston Smith, slowly begins to secretly rebel against the system.

It's one of the most impactful satires in all literature, an absolutely creative marvel that warns us about oppression and mass surveillance, and remains just as relevant and terrifying now as it was when it was released in 1949. It's an absolute must-read for more than just sci-fi fans, as it's perfectly structured and has a powerful message that carries with it much urgency.

'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sleep?' (1968)

Image via Doubleday

From renowned sci-fi novelist Philip K. Dick comes his legendary masterpiece, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?. This profound and masterful story laid the groundwork for the cyberpunk sci-fi genre, laying down the foundation that so many novels, movies, and video games would build from. Set in the post-apocalyptic future of San Francisco, reclusive bounty hunter Rick Deckard is tasked with killing six rouge androids running loose in the city that have started forming their own independent identities.

Packed with sharp writing, a brilliant pace, and some of the most thought-provoking themes ever told in a book, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is an undeniable staple of the genre that has remained consistently relevant and timeless over the years. items.title: Eternally Yours asks: What if Ghosts, but vampires?
items.author: Matt Webb Mitovich
items.summary: Some ideas, like immortal creatures of the night, just refuse to die. Joe Port and Joe Wiseman first pitched their new supernatural comedy, Eternally Yours, 11
items.text:
Some ideas, like immortal creatures of the night, just refuse to die. Joe Port and Joe Wiseman first pitched their new supernatural comedy, Eternally Yours, 11 years ago, but it didn’t get past the pilot stage—though that was before Port and Wiseman successfully adapted BBC One’s Ghosts for CBS. Between their shared creative braintrust and the 8:30 p.m. Thursday time slot Eternally Yours is about to stake out—save for a pair of holiday specials, Ghosts won’t be back with season 6 until early next year—it’s clear someone’s hoping that viewers draw a line between these two shows. And that’s before you even get into the contents of Eternally Yours, which is, to put it bluntly, “What if Ghosts, but vampires?”


Eternally Yours stars Ed Weeks and Allegra Edwards as Charles and Liz Blythe, lovebirds in 1526 Austria who pledge their lives to one another when he, a vampire, sinks his fangs into her waiting, mortal neck. Thing is, 500 years is a really long time to be married to the same person, they’ve come to realize, and as such we find Charles and Liz in a bit of a rut as the series opens. Helen J. Shen plays the couple’s daughter Emma, adopted but also a vampire—what, you have a better cure for diphtheria?—and she can’t bring herself to tell her folks that she is dating a regular ol’, employed-by-the-Social Security Administration human. When said beau, Max (Jaren Lewison), coincidentally finds himself at the Blythes’ doorstep on official SSA business—whoops, someone has been collecting benefits for far too many decades—it’s not long before he learns their bloody surprising secret. That sounds like a spoiler, but it’s not. Nor is it the biggest twist in the first and only episode available for review.


The Blythe coven is also comprised of Jesse (Parker Young), a fitness trainer who spray tans so as to not disappear in the gym’s mirrors, and his wife Phyllis (the hilarious Rose Abdoo), who is kept oblivious to the household’s vampire situation via frequent mind wipes. That wonderfully odd couple has a pair of teenage sons, Henry and Mort—the former a tortured brooder à la Edward Cullen, the latter frustrated that his only super power is to read the mind of Argus, the family dog. Not exciting stuff, that.


Eternally Yours allows itself a major liberty when it comes to vampire lore: the Blythes are able to roam about in the daylight, though it significantly helps that they live in famously overcast Seattle. And yet the pilot episode, at least, feels terribly claustrophobic, with a majority of its scenes confined to the Blythe house. One could argue that Ghosts has managed to deal with this very same obstacle, as its titular spooks are bound to the property where they died. It raises the question of what future episodes of Eternally Yours will look like, though Port recently assured reporters that with Charles employed as a financial advisor, Liz a college professor, and Emma a veterinarian, we will see these characters out in the world, living their afterlives.


Arriving nearly two years after FX’s What We Do In The Shadows concluded its lauded, six-season run, Eternally Yours faces a “Simpsons Already Did It” conundrum in that much fun has already been made and had by vampires laying low in suburbia. (Case in point, the logline for the October 22 episode has the Blythes hosting a party attended by esteemed members of their vampire community. How will Emmy-winning guest star Jeff Hiller stack up against Shadows‘ Doug Jones?) But there’s a lighter, brighter “network sitcom” sensibility at play here that portends to set Eternally Yours apart.


“Life is tough, and then you continue to not die,” Charles tells Emma as she laments centuries of dating travails. A beat later, when Liz reminds Emma that one of her past boyfriends fed on a mailman instead of, as is their ethical preference, a “bad” person, Charles sniffs, “They can’t always be the worst of the worst.”


Eternally Yours shows promise, though one has to wonder why Max is clued into Emma’s family secret so early on. Similarly, a closing twist feels more like the stinger to a season finale. Is the freshman comedy ticking obvious boxes too quickly? Time will tell. And being immortal, the Blythes have all the time in the world.


Eternally Yours premieres Thursday, October 8 at 8:30 p.m. ET on CBS.

items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: In the grim darkness of the far future, there is something far worse than war. There is: a level that is basically a huge, spinning lock full of tentacles,
items.text:
In the grim darkness of the far future, there is something far worse than war. There is: a level that is basically a huge, spinning lock full of tentacles, with your Space Marine or Sister of Battle protagonist naturally serving as the key.

Auroch Digital's new FPS Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 launches next week, and I've been chatting to the game's principal designer Matt Bone about some of the more "creative" environments in store. It's a sturdy rule of thumb that all the best ideas in gamedev are the ones that make your colleagues want to fill your trousers with sea urchins. Bone certainly appears to have achieved this with the map comfortingly known as Vicious Circles.

Watch on YouTube

"One of the things we wanted to do with Boltgun 2 is add more variety," he told me over email. "Part of that is more diverse and exotic biomes, and another part is introducing novel mechanics. The level 'Vicious Circles' is a great example of this, and definitely one of the more challenging levels to make. The informal name the team uses for the level is 'Puzzle Box', as it's made up of a series of connected, rotating 'ring' sections, as well as a giant, slowly spinning cog that acts as the finale of the level. The player moves one of the rings at different points in the levels, unlocking different areas so that they can progress (or explore for secrets).

"These moving sections are covered in enemies and pickups, which is part of the reason coders will never forgive me for this level," Bone went on. "Getting enemies to reliably navigate and fight the player on moving, interconnected platforms is a bit of a headache, as you can imagine. And spinning a gigantic cog covered in hundreds of meshes is quite the performance challenge."

Not content with alienating the coders, Bone has also managed to earn the eternal enmity of the art team. The Vicious Circles level is set in a spaceship belonging to Boltgun 2's primary antagonist Vashtorr, a demigod who – as is often the pastime of Chaos denizens – really enjoys building machines out of body parts and vice versa. "We really leaned into this 'fleshmetal' aspect for the environment, which looks incredible and appropriately disturbing," Bone went on. "But the reason artists now also hate me is that all of this intricate level art has to work in multiple configurations, not just one. A wriggling fleshy tendril may look perfect in the original level layout, but has to then avoid clipping through walls in the level's various rotations."

"Whilst it was certainly a challenge, I absolutely think it was worth it," he concluded, with the resolute good cheer of a man reconciled to his own damnation. "Hopefully it'll be a memorable level for players!"

Speaking as one such feckless player, I feel no sympathy for Auroch Digital's rank-and-file. I've just been reading the papers, and according to some columnist or other, you've all been 'corrupting the children' - being forced to make a massive Merry-go-Round out of gall bladders is no more than you deserve. Also, I really like videogame levels that are ginormous machines, such as the Clockwork Mansion in Dishonored 2, or Anoat City (kind of) in Star Wars: Dark Forces, or Into The Abyss from Titanfall 2. Any other favourite or especially loathed examples to share?

Read more about Boltgun 2 on Steam. Here is what Caelyn thought of the first: "A fast and joyously entertaining rampage through a spot-on recreation of the Warhammer 40,000 setting, Boltgun is the FPS that 40k fans have dreamed of since the first time they inexpertly splodged too-thick paint all over a Space Marine. Pacing issues can’t prevent it from being a bloody good time."
