While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. This term is a great example of words being traded back and forth between two languages.

14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.

28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”

Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.

As a matter of fact, Japanese doesn’t just borrow words from English. To find out more, read our blog: Loan Words in Japanese that Don’t Come from English!

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).
18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”
19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.
Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts
From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.
20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).
21. Noh　(能)
In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.
22. Tanka　(短歌)
A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.
23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.
Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.
23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.
Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.
25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.
26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.
27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.
28. Zen　(善)
This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.
29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.
30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.
31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.
32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.
Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.
33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.
34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.
35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”
Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.
As a matter of fact, Japanese doesn’t just borrow words from English. To find out more, read our blog: Loan Words in Japanese that Don’t Come from English!

Yes, English language borrows a lot of Japanese words. For example, tsunami, tycoon and sudoku came from the Japanese equivalent. English language also retains a lot of original Japanese food-related words, like sushi, katsu and dashi.

items.text:
If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest question, and probably the most important. Between people’s fascination with Japanese culture and the desire to live in Japan, Japanese has become one of the most popular languages to learn – but also the hardest, too.

The answer to this question is, “it depends”. Understandably, no one likes to hear that — but it’s an honest answer because there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to how long it takes to learn Japanese. On a complete beginner-to-advanced scale, it takes around 180 to 1,2000 hours to learn Japanese. In reality, people with no prior kanji knowledge often take more time to learn Japanese thanthose who have.

In this response, we’ll explore the factors that can affect how long it takes to learn Japanese and provide estimates of how long it may take a beginner to become proficient.

Defining Fluency in Japanese Language Learning

To the majority, language fluency is a spectrum. You can talk to your Japanese friends in casual Japanese and call it fluent. You might think that to be one means being able to lead a meeting with your coworkers in full keigo.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.

So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.

How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.

GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours

TravelAsk for directions, order food, and make basic greetings.7 – 30 days

Make friendsDaily conversations, expressing thoughts and opinions, holding natural conversations in a wider range of circumstances.900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Work part-time job in JapanSpeak basic keigo to customers, interact with Japanese coworkers900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Get a job in JapanTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination) and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, and make a presentation2,000 – 4,000 study hours (2 years)

Go to universityTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination, and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, make a presentationUse keigo (Japanese honorifics), business Japanese, manners, and cultural awareness, JLPT (N2 or N1)

How Many Hours a Day Should You Study Japanese

You might notice we’ve been using “study hours” instead of exact days or months, which can be frustrating if you want a straightforward answer on how long it takes to learn Japanese.

Days and months can vary in length and can be influenced by external factors, such as holidays or personal schedules, making it difficult to accurately track progress. There are people who might study 30 minutes a day. Some dedicate 3 hours a day, while a few people spend 6-7 hours studying full-time. This isn’t the best standardized unit of time.

If you are learning as a hobby, dedicating 15 to 30 minutes a day to studying is fine. In 6 months, you’ll be able to read basic texts and hold limited conversations.

Most people recommend studying for 3 to 4 hours every day on a set schedule, which allows your brain to work at its full capacity and avoid burnout. Even intensive courses at Coto Academy and Japanese language classes at other Japanese language schools only have 3-hour classes on weekdays.

So if you think studying 9 hours a day to achieve the “study hour goal” is a good idea, think again! You’ll most likely experience burnout and have trouble holding onto the information that you have learned.

Head here full our guide on how long it takes to study for each JLPT level!

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Beginner

When we think of Japanese levels, we tend to associate it with JLPT, or the Japanese Language Proficiency Test, as the ultimate benchmark for how much Japanese you know. Beginner-level Japanese ranges from JLPT N5 (beginner) to N4 (upper beginner).

According to the official JLPT administrator, JLPT N5 and N4 “prove your ability to understand some basic Japanese.” You should be able to listen and comprehend conversations about daily life and classroom situations — provided that they are spoken slowly.

Reading-wise, this means you’re already familiar with daily topics written in basic vocabulary and kanji.

For students with kanji knowledge, it takes 350 study hours to pass JLPT N5, and 462 hours if you have no prior kanji knowledge. For JLPT N4, it will take 550 hours and 787 hours under the same conditions.

Keep in mind that the JLPT does not test your conversational skills, so while your written Japanese skills are good, this doesn’t necessarily reflect your practical fluency during day-to-day conversations.

If you want to learn the most basic kanji and have no prior experience with Japanese, it should take you around a month. This is if you learn 10 kanji a day every day.

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Intermediate

Japanese intermediate level is around JLPT N3, which can take 900 – 1,500 study hours to get to. Many Japanese learners are at this level, and you should be able to get a part-time job at this point. You are able to get around Japan with ease, and while you may still encounter difficulties in understanding and expressing certain ideas, you should be able to engage in conversations on a wide range of topics with a degree of fluency and accuracy.

Typically, studying for JLPT N3 takes about 6 months to one year, depending on how many hours you dedicate each day and how hard you commit to your study plan.

Around N3, you should already know around 650 kanji, which can take anywhere from 2 months to four months if you learn 5-10 kanji each day.

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Advanced

In order to get a high level of Japanese proficiency for work, you’ll want to achieve JLPT N1 and have sufficient written and spoken ability to effectively communicate in various settings, such as in-person interactions, emails, presentations, and meetings, with a mastery of the formal Japanese register (keigo). Acquiring the JLPT N2 or N1 certification can take anywhere from 2,200 hours to 3,900 hours of study, which would require at least 2 years of full-time study. Even after obtaining an N1 certification, many learners continue to study more kanji and vocabulary to further improve their proficiency.

You can achieve the same advanced level in 3-5 years of learning Japanese part-time. This is when you can get jobs that require native-level Japanese skills, like interpreters, translators, customer service, and Japanese teachers.

In most cases, the amount of exposure to the Japanese language and culture plays a big part in truly reaching an advanced level. At this point, it’s not just about knowing a lot of grammar points, vocabulary, or kanji; it’s also about understanding the culture and context in which the language is used.

Ways to Speed up Japanese Learning

Most of us have different learning preferences, like taking notes, using visuals or graphics, or speaking words out loud. There are numerous ways to acquire proficiency in Japanese, but selecting the most effective method for yourself will enable you to enhance your learning speed and quality. Here are a few tips we always recommend to those who are starting to learn Japanese.

1. Find a language partner

Studying alone can be boring unless you’re an introvert. Not only does it provide an opportunity to practice speaking and listening in a natural setting, but it also offers insight into Japanese culture, values, and customs. Interacting with native speakers can expose you to a variety of regional dialects, idiomatic expressions, and slang that are not commonly found in textbooks or language courses. Moreover, it allows you to receive immediate feedback on your language usage, pronunciation, and grammar, which is invaluable in accelerating your language acquisition.

Engaging in conversations with Japanese friends or exchange partners can also make language learning more enjoyable, provide new social connections, and lead to a deeper understanding and appreciation of Japanese culture. We recommend checking out our curated list of Japanese language exchange apps and where to find language exchange events.

2. Study Japanese in Japan for Total Immersion

This one is probably obvious, but hear us out: you learn Japanese most effectively when you’re studying the language in Japan — or at least when you are constantly exposed to Japanese culture. Besides, what better way to reward yourself for your hard work than to visit a country we all love?

Immersing yourself in Japanese culture and making friends with native speakers can be almost impossible outside Japan. Being in Japan will boost your progress considerably. You’re conditioned to always use Japanese, and you’ll inevitably hear Japanese words and phrases every day.

3. Define your motivation and goal

Want to learn Japanese as a hobby? Find new job opportunities in Japan from overseas? Watch your favorite anime. It’s good to define your goal in learning Japanese for a couple of reasons; the first being that these goals are your motivators. A lot of people lose interest in learning Japanese because it gets too hard or boring. Knowing why you want to study in the first place helps you to keep the traction going.

Second, and probably more importantly, it helps you identify which language element you need to focus on. Learning Japanese to take the JLPT for university entrance? You should do a well-balanced study plan covering listening, speaking, reading, and vocabulary. Want to be able to make small talk? Try to do more conversation practice instead.

4. Use a mix of Japanese study materials

Perhaps you’re an auditory learner. Or maybe you notice you hate using textbooks. No matter what kind of Japanese learner you are, studying Japanese can be more effective when you’re genuinely enjoying it — or even making it fun!

And the good news is, you can learn from things you already enjoy in Japanese. For example, if you like playing video games, you can switch the language to Japanese, especially with games like Pokémon, where the language is simple and easy to change when starting a new game.

Enjoy reading manga? Challenge yourself to read a bit each day in Japanese, and as you progress, it will become easier. Additionally, watching your favorite shows in Japanese, like anime series or Terrace House on Netflix, is a fun way to pick up new vocabulary and slang. Initially, try watching without subtitles and actively listening, taking notes, and then watching again with subtitles on to see what you understood and learned.

We have a huge list of articles dedicated to different learning resources: Anki, podcasts, YouTube, TikToks and TV shows, so check them out on our blog!

5. Join a Japanese course

It’s important not to overlook the significance of getting the right professional support and establishing a study routine. This is where taking a Japanese course comes in.

One of the main benefits of taking a Japanese class is having access to a qualified instructor who can answer questions, provide feedback, and offer guidance tailored to your individual needs. Additionally, studying with a group of peers can create a sense of accountability and motivation, as well as the opportunity to practice speaking and listening skills with others.

If you’re considering taking a Japanese class, we recommend checking out Coto Academy. They offer a wide range of courses, from beginner to advanced levels, taught by experienced and knowledgeable instructors. Their curriculum is designed to be engaging and interactive, and they use a variety of teaching methods to cater to different learning styles. Additionally, their flexible scheduling options and online classes make it easy to fit language learning into your busy schedule.


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


Conclusion

Learning to speak Japanese involves many factors, but by developing good study habits, managing your time effectively, and staying committed, you can become conversational in a few months. This may come as a surprise, as you may have had different expectations about the process of learning Japanese.

It’s important to find joy and a sense of satisfaction throughout your journey, not just at the end goal. Celebrate each small accomplishment along the way and try not to focus too much on how far you still have to go. One day, you’ll be glad that you persevered and didn’t give up!

How long does it take to learn Japanese for beginners?


The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. However, the amount of time it takes to learn Japanese for beginners depends on various factors, such as how often and how long you study, the quality of your study materials, your motivation, and your natural ability to learn languages.

How many hours a day should I study Japanese to become fluent?

The number of hours a day you need to study Japanese to become fluent depends on your personal goals, your current level of proficiency, and your preferred learning style. Generally, it’s recommended to study at least 1-2 hours a day, every day, to make steady progress. As a reference, intensive Japanese courses typically 3 hours a day. Studying 6 hours or more in a day may lead to burnout.

Can I become fluent in Japanese in six months?


While it’s possible to make significant progress in six months of intensive study, becoming fully fluent in Japanese within such a short period is unlikely. Achieving fluency in Japanese requires a deep understanding of the language, which takes time to develop. You can achieve conversational fluency in six months.

How long does it take to pass the JLPT N5, N4, N3, N2 or N1 level?


On average, it takes 6 months to 1 year of dedicated study to pass each level of the JLPT. However, some people may take longer or shorter depending on their individual circumstances.

Can I learn Japanese faster with a tutor or language exchange partner?


Working with a tutor or language exchange partner can help you learn Japanese faster and more effectively. A tutor can provide personalized instruction and feedback, while a language exchange partner can offer opportunities to practice speaking and listening skills with a native speaker.

How long does it take to learn Japanese kanji?


On average, it takes about 2-3 years of consistent study to master the basic set of 2,136 Joyo kanji (commonly used characters in Japan).

Can I learn Japanese on my own without a teacher?


Yes, it’s possible to learn Japanese on your own without a teacher. However, self-study requires a lot of discipline, motivation, and the right resources. You’ll need to find quality textbooks, online resources, and study materials, and you’ll need to develop a consistent study routine to make progress.

Is it difficult to learn Japanese compared to other languages?


Japanese is considered to be a logical and consistent language with a relatively simple sound system, but it’s considered one of the hardest languages to learn for English speakers. FSI considered Japanese a “super-hard language”, categorizing it in the same group as Arabic, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.
So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.
How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.
GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours
TravelAsk for directions, order food, and make basic greetings.7 – 30 days
Make friendsDaily conversations, expressing thoughts and opinions, holding natural conversations in a wider range of circumstances.900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)
Work part-time job in JapanSpeak basic keigo to customers, interact with Japanese coworkers900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

How Many Hours a Day Should You Study Japanese
You might notice we’ve been using “study hours” instead of exact days or months, which can be frustrating if you want a straightforward answer on how long it takes to learn Japanese.

Days and months can vary in length and can be influenced by external factors, such as holidays or personal schedules, making it difficult to accurately track progress. There are people who might study 30 minutes a day. Some dedicate 3 hours a day, while a few people spend 6-7 hours studying full-time. This isn’t the best standardized unit of time.
If you are learning as a hobby, dedicating 15 to 30 minutes a day to studying is fine. In 6 months, you’ll be able to read basic texts and hold limited conversations.

Most people recommend studying for 3 to 4 hours every day on a set schedule, which allows your brain to work at its full capacity and avoid burnout. Even intensive courses at Coto Academy and Japanese language classes at other Japanese language schools only have 3-hour classes on weekdays.

So if you think studying 9 hours a day to achieve the “study hour goal” is a good idea, think again! You’ll most likely experience burnout and have trouble holding onto the information that you have learned.
Head here full our guide on how long it takes to study for each JLPT level!
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Beginner

When we think of Japanese levels, we tend to associate it with JLPT, or the Japanese Language Proficiency Test, as the ultimate benchmark for how much Japanese you know. Beginner-level Japanese ranges from JLPT N5 (beginner) to N4 (upper beginner).

According to the official JLPT administrator, JLPT N5 and N4 “prove your ability to understand some basic Japanese.” You should be able to listen and comprehend conversations about daily life and classroom situations — provided that they are spoken slowly.
Reading-wise, this means you’re already familiar with daily topics written in basic vocabulary and kanji.

For students with kanji knowledge, it takes 350 study hours to pass JLPT N5, and 462 hours if you have no prior kanji knowledge. For JLPT N4, it will take 550 hours and 787 hours under the same conditions.

Keep in mind that the JLPT does not test your conversational skills, so while your written Japanese skills are good, this doesn’t necessarily reflect your practical fluency during day-to-day conversations.
If you want to learn the most basic kanji and have no prior experience with Japanese, it should take you around a month. This is if you learn 10 kanji a day every day.
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Intermediate

Japanese intermediate level is around JLPT N3, which can take 900 – 1,500 study hours to get to. Many Japanese learners are at this level, and you should be able to get a part-time job at this point. You are able to get around Japan with ease, and while you may still encounter difficulties in understanding and expressing certain ideas, you should be able to engage in conversations on a wide range of topics with a degree of fluency and accuracy.
Typically, studying for JLPT N3 takes about 6 months to one year, depending on how many hours you dedicate each day and how hard you commit to your study plan.
Around N3, you should already know around 650 kanji, which can take anywhere from 2 months to four months if you learn 5-10 kanji each day.
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Advanced

In order to get a high level of Japanese proficiency for work, you’ll want to achieve JLPT N1 and have sufficient written and spoken ability to effectively communicate in various settings, such as in-person interactions, emails, presentations, and meetings, with a mastery of the formal Japanese register (keigo). Acquiring the JLPT N2 or N1 certification can take anywhere from 2,200 hours to 3,900 hours of study, which would require at least 2 years of full-time study. Even after obtaining an N1 certification, many learners continue to study more kanji and vocabulary to further improve their proficiency.

You can achieve the same advanced level in 3-5 years of learning Japanese part-time. This is when you can get jobs that require native-level Japanese skills, like interpreters, translators, customer service, and Japanese teachers.

In most cases, the amount of exposure to the Japanese language and culture plays a big part in truly reaching an advanced level. At this point, it’s not just about knowing a lot of grammar points, vocabulary, or kanji; it’s also about understanding the culture and context in which the language is used.
Ways to Speed up Japanese Learning

Most of us have different learning preferences, like taking notes, using visuals or graphics, or speaking words out loud. There are numerous ways to acquire proficiency in Japanese, but selecting the most effective method for yourself will enable you to enhance your learning speed and quality. Here are a few tips we always recommend to those who are starting to learn Japanese.
1. Find a language partner

Studying alone can be boring unless you’re an introvert. Not only does it provide an opportunity to practice speaking and listening in a natural setting, but it also offers insight into Japanese culture, values, and customs. Interacting with native speakers can expose you to a variety of regional dialects, idiomatic expressions, and slang that are not commonly found in textbooks or language courses. Moreover, it allows you to receive immediate feedback on your language usage, pronunciation, and grammar, which is invaluable in accelerating your language acquisition.

Engaging in conversations with Japanese friends or exchange partners can also make language learning more enjoyable, provide new social connections, and lead to a deeper understanding and appreciation of Japanese culture. We recommend checking out our curated list of Japanese language exchange apps and where to find language exchange events.
2. Study Japanese in Japan for Total Immersion

This one is probably obvious, but hear us out: you learn Japanese most effectively when you’re studying the language in Japan — or at least when you are constantly exposed to Japanese culture. Besides, what better way to reward yourself for your hard work than to visit a country we all love?

Immersing yourself in Japanese culture and making friends with native speakers can be almost impossible outside Japan. Being in Japan will boost your progress considerably. You’re conditioned to always use Japanese, and you’ll inevitably hear Japanese words and phrases every day.
3. Define your motivation and goal

Want to learn Japanese as a hobby? Find new job opportunities in Japan from overseas? Watch your favorite anime. It’s good to define your goal in learning Japanese for a couple of reasons; the first being that these goals are your motivators. A lot of people lose interest in learning Japanese because it gets too hard or boring. Knowing why you want to study in the first place helps you to keep the traction going.

Second, and probably more importantly, it helps you identify which language element you need to focus on. Learning Japanese to take the JLPT for university entrance? You should do a well-balanced study plan covering listening, speaking, reading, and vocabulary. Want to be able to make small talk? Try to do more conversation practice instead.
4. Use a mix of Japanese study materials

Perhaps you’re an auditory learner. Or maybe you notice you hate using textbooks. No matter what kind of Japanese learner you are, studying Japanese can be more effective when you’re genuinely enjoying it — or even making it fun!

And the good news is, you can learn from things you already enjoy in Japanese. For example, if you like playing video games, you can switch the language to Japanese, especially with games like Pokémon, where the language is simple and easy to change when starting a new game.

Enjoy reading manga? Challenge yourself to read a bit each day in Japanese, and as you progress, it will become easier. Additionally, watching your favorite shows in Japanese, like anime series or Terrace House on Netflix, is a fun way to pick up new vocabulary and slang. Initially, try watching without subtitles and actively listening, taking notes, and then watching again with subtitles on to see what you understood and learned.
We have a huge list of articles dedicated to different learning resources: Anki, podcasts, YouTube, TikToks and TV shows, so check them out on our blog!
5. Join a Japanese course
It’s important not to overlook the significance of getting the right professional support and establishing a study routine. This is where taking a Japanese course comes in.

One of the main benefits of taking a Japanese class is having access to a qualified instructor who can answer questions, provide feedback, and offer guidance tailored to your individual needs. Additionally, studying with a group of peers can create a sense of accountability and motivation, as well as the opportunity to practice speaking and listening skills with others.

Their curriculum is designed to be engaging and interactive, and they use a variety of teaching methods to cater to different learning styles. Additionally, their flexible scheduling options and online classes make it easy to fit language learning into your busy schedule.

Conclusion

Learning to speak Japanese involves many factors, but by developing good study habits, managing your time effectively, and staying committed, you can become conversational in a few months. This may come as a surprise, as you may have had different expectations about the process of learning Japanese.

It’s important to find joy and a sense of satisfaction throughout your journey, not just at the end goal. Celebrate each small accomplishment along the way and try not to focus too much on how far you still have to go. One day, you’ll be glad that you persevered and didn’t give up!

items.text:
Be warned: you are about to read the most groan-worthy Japanese dad jokes ever! 親父ギャグ (Oyaji gyagu), literally meaning “old man gags,” is the Japanese equivalent of “dad jokes.” They are characterized by cheesy puns, or ダジャレ in Japanese. Similar to English, Japanese puns are built on homophones, or words that sound the same but have different meanings.

Dad jokes are just as cheesy in Japanese as they are in any language, but they are a great way to learn about Japanese culture and humor while practicing informal sentence structures. Japanese dad jokes can help with picking up natural language through their use of non-literal, figurative language.

What Are Japanese Dad Jokes or 親父ギャグ (Oyaji Gagu)?

Most Japanese dad jokes use homophones, a fancy grammatical term for when two different words, with different meanings, sound very similar. Since the Japanese language only has a limited number of unique syllables to build words from, homophones end up being very common, and it’s quite easy to make corny jokes out of them. This is the basis of many dad jokes and ダジャレ in general.

Onomatopoeia, or the written form of action sounds, are abundant in the Japanese language, so they are another common component of dad jokes.

1. このステーキはすてき！(kono suteeki wa suteki!)

Romaji: Kono suteeki wa suteki!
Meaning: The steak is wonderful!
Joke Explanation:
Steak → ステーキ (suteeki)
Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.

2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)

The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.

3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.

4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)

This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!

5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる

6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.

7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.

8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.

To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.

9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.

10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.

How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes

Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.


Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.

Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.

Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.


Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!

Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!

Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!

Showing your sense of humor is essential for natural Japanese fluency! Join our conversation-focused Japanese courses to learn to speak Japanese confidently and even joke around with friends! We offer flexible, part-time classes as well as intensive classes at a variety of levels.

Whether you’re starting from scratch or you want to take your Japanese to the next level, we have a class for you! Visit one of our campuses in Tokyo or Yokohama, or join online from anywhere around the world!

Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.
2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)
The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.
3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.
4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)
This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!
5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる
6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.
7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.
8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.
To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.
9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.
10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.
How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes
Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.
Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.
Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.
Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.
Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!
Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!
Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!
